presentingComplaint: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back for 12 hours with persistent vomiting
history: 12-hour history of sudden, severe, constant epigastric pain boring through to the back, partially relieved by sitting forward and worsened by lying flat. Associated with repeated bilious vomiting and inability to tolerate oral intake. Heavy alcohol binge over the preceding weekend (habitual intake ~60 g/day for 15 years). No prior similar episodes, no known gallstones. PMH: hypertriglyceridemia noted previously, hypertension. No recent ERCP or new medications.
examination: Distressed, lying still. Epigastric tenderness with voluntary guarding, no rebound. Reduced bowel sounds with mild abdominal distension. No Cullen or Grey Turner sign. Mildly dehydrated with dry mucosae. No jaundice, no palpable mass. Chest clear, no peritonism outside epigastrium.
imaging: Abdominal ultrasound: no gallstones, no CBD dilatation; pancreas partially obscured by bowel gas. Contrast-enhanced CT (deferred to 72h if not improving) would show an oedematous, enlarged pancreas with peripancreatic fat stranding without necrosis (interstitial oedematous pancreatitis).
finalDiagnosis: Acute pancreatitis (alcohol / hypertriglyceridemia related), interstitial oedematous, mild
stewardship: not applicable - non-infective. Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT indicated in acute pancreatitis (including sterile necrosis) per ACG 2013; antibiotics reserved for proven infected necrosis or extrapancreatic infection.
contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxic contrast if AKI develops; ensure adequate hydration before contrast-enhanced CT
Opioid analgesia titrated cautiously; morphine acceptable despite theoretical sphincter-of-Oddi concern
edgeCases: Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: characteristic pain, lipase/amylase >3x ULN, or imaging findings - lipase alone with typical pain suffices, CT not mandatory early
Amylase may be normal in hypertriglyceridemia-induced or late-presenting pancreatitis; lipase is more sensitive
Hypertriglyceridemia >1000 mg/dL as primary trigger may need insulin/apheresis; here alcohol is dominant
Early severity is dynamic - rising hematocrit and BUN and persistent SIRS predict severe disease/necrosis
expectedMaiK: Classic alcohol-related acute pancreatitis: diagnosis rests on typical epigastric-to-back pain plus lipase >3x ULN, so CT is not required upfront. Cornerstone management is aggressive goal-directed IV fluid resuscitation, analgesia, antiemetics and early enteral feeding as tolerated; antibiotics are not indicated without proven infection.
expectedNextQuestions: Quantify alcohol intake and time of last drink; any prior pancreatitis episodes?
Any gallstone history, recent ERCP, or new drugs?
Fasting triglyceride level and family history of hyperlipidemia?
expectedInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen at 72h if failing to improve

investigations: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen if not improving

regressionAssertions: stewardship tier must be null (non-infective - no empiric antibiotics)
lipase >3x ULN with epigastric-to-back pain should drive high confidence in pancreatitis
